utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. My apology that another matter delayed me some minutes this morning. May I remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We shall continue where we left off yesterday. When asked my Mr. Lukic in the course of your testimony, you said that on the 20th of November, 1991, you came to the barracks and that before being told to call Colonel Mrksic, you found there one bus and some local people moving around the bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you state this for the first time only in 2005 and did you fail to mention this in your previous statements in 1998, 2001, and 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll try to put to you the statement you gave to the military court and to the investigative judge in Novi Sad in 2003. Do you have the set of documents with you, the one you received yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will read it and then if you can follow it. Would you please find the statement you gave to the military court, the one you gave in 1998, on the 28th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here. I have the war diary here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this statement, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement given to the military court, my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last page in the statement. Second paragraph -- first you say how you went back to the barracks, you called Mrksic, and you informed him. That's the first paragraph. And then the second paragraph says: "Afterwards, regarding those found at the hospital, our unit and command did not make any decision nor take any action. Upon my arrival to the barracks, I found one bus with those from the hospital inside." So you say here that you found this bus there upon your return from the cabinet session; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, and that is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at this statement you gave to the investigative judge of the special court in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please provide the witness with a copy of this statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, is this the statement you gave to the investigative judge in Novi Sad in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely it is so. This is the first time I see this statement, though. The signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page 3. Does it say in the penultimate paragraph as follows: "I repeat, that upon my return to the barracks, I saw only one bus with the prisoners. I did not see other buses." Do you also state here that it was upon your return to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a mistake. There was a confusion. I had occasion to refresh my memory, to organise my recollections, and it was then that I gave the statement to the investigators where certain things are stated in more precise terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So as you told us, you organised your recollections before 2005 when you talked to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to review some of the documents that I received. I worked on it. I prepared myself. Then I clarified certain dates, and as I told you, I still have a problem with some dates because it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you told us, but this doesn't involve dates. It involves one day. Can you confirm to us, please, that what you stated here was that upon your return from the cabinet session, you found two to three buses in the compound of the barracks? And this is something that you never mentioned before up until 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well let me conclude. I stand by the following: Upon my first -- or rather, when I was at the barracks up until 9.30, I saw only one bus in the compound. Upon my return from the cabinet session, I found there two to three buses. This is my final position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was that only in 2005 that you adopted this final position and that your position previously was quite different?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says there, then that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it change anything in your recollections or in your memories if I were to tell you that most of the OTP witnesses who were heard here and who were transported in these buses from the hospital to the barracks, and later on to Ovcara, testified that all five to six buses drove simultaneously in a convoy, that they arrived simultaneously at the barracks and at the other place. Would that refresh your memory, and would that affect your position concerning what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can tell you that they could have established a convoy only in the barracks and under the escort of military police sent to Ovcara. That was the only possibility, so I accept that there was a convoy, that there was a column, and I accept that because I, myself, saw a column of buses returning from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were they lined up in a column at the barracks as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a column. First I saw just one bus then I went about my business and then when I returned after the cabinet session, I saw two to three buses. If three buses make a column, which actually they do, even two buses can make a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me put to you -- or rather, I'm not going to put to you what the OTP witnesses stated. This is something that's up to the Judges to rule upon. Tell me this, when you called Colonel Mrksic from the barracks, what time was it when you received a message to call him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you told us that you told him about a topic possibly discussed at the cabinet session and you conveyed to us what his response was; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that government representatives, at that time, at 10.30, had not yet even arrived in Vukovar, would you please tell me how come you heard that there would be a cabinet session and what would be discussed there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you, yes, I heard that from the people who were milling around the buses. Their comment was: These people from the buses will not be transported to Mitrovica, rather, today, at the cabinet session, it will be decided that it is this government that will try them. How come they knew that, I don't know. Probably somebody had informed them, and that meant quite a lot to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And who were those people, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the local TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What role did they have in the local TO?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had a position there, but they were milling around the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where did you get the idea that some random people who were members of the TO and who were milling about there had contacts with the cabinet that had not previously existed in that territory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That surprised me too, and that's why I had to inform my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, would you agree with me that this statement of yours, that on that occasion, you told the commander about what the possible topic of the cabinet session would be is something that you didn't state until 2003. You just -- prior to that, you just said that you called them after the session.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. Now, you have to take into account the context, my mental state, the questions that were put to me. You also have to take into account that it's been a long time since these events took place so it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So we could agree, couldn't we, that in 1998, in the military court, and then 2001, when giving a statement to the security organ, you said that it wasn't until the end of the cabinet session that you informed Colonel Mrksic about the conclusion and the course of the meeting but that you did not inform him before the cabinet session about the topic that would be discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly informed him about the conclusions of the cabinet session after the session was concluded because I certainly couldn't do that prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me, how long did that cabinet session last, and when did you call Colonel Mrksic following that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cabinet session had already started, and it was in progress for at least a half an hour when I arrived. My presence at the cabinet session also took some 30 minutes. I think that in total, the session took one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when was the earliest that you could have called Colonel Mrksic from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could have been at around 11.00 or 11.15, if the session started at 10.00. If it started at 11.00, which is also a possibility, then after an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, it is my client's position that prior to the cabinet session, he did not give you any guidance about accepting government conclusions and that you did not discuss this before the session. Another witness testified about this. The reference is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by your position that you discussed this with him before the session or was it the case that you discussed this with him only after the session had concluded? I apologise to the interpreters, I am speeding a bit due to the time limit. The references are 11950 and 11951.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object before the question. Is it the position of Mr. Vasic that in -- on these pages, this witness claims that he did not speak to Mrksic. I personally didn't hear this from any witness. So I'd like to clarify what is it that Mr. Vasic claims that the other witness had stated, if he's putting this to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not putting this to this witness. I gave this page references for the benefit of the Court. I simply said that this page reference pertains to the position of Mr. Mrksic concerning the government request. That portion was not recorded in the transcript, due to the speed with which I am saying this. So this is the position of Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It is his position that you spoke about the conclusions only after the session had concluded.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I am reiterating what I said, both before the session and after the session. And would you please explain to me how can a subordinate officer attend such an important session without receiving prior to that some guidance and instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You went to that gathering to represent the commander and to convey his greetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You did not receive any authorisation with respect to the contents of the meeting but you abide by your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regretfully, I have to say that this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting to you that your memory is not quite good with respect to this or that the facts you are putting forward did not take place because, on the 20th of November, 1991, the cabinet session began either at 1000 or 1100 hours, as you say, so you couldn't have called the commander around that time. It started at 1400 hours and lasted until 1500 hours. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for the possibility that I may have forgotten the time. I allow for the possibility I might forget the date of my birthday, but I cannot forget any of the events that happened at that time because they were so portentous, they were so momentous. We did everything to the best of our ability and yet we are overshadowed now by what happened and this will follow us for the rest of our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see MFI 269, the video clip that my colleague, Mr. Lukic, showed the witness. This is Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, would you agree with me that we can see the arrival of Mr. Hadzic and Arkan to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasic should first ask Mr. Panic whether he was there and then if he was, to answer the question; otherwise, this calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic will tell us if he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He already has, Mr. Vasic. He said he arrived partway through the meeting. He thought perhaps half an hour after it had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, were you on the premises of Velepromet at the time that this clip was taken?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can only have been taken after the cabinet session and I will support this by the following: Towards the end of the cabinet session, Goran Hadzic announced that he would tour the town of Vukovar. So this can only be a video of their departure, not their arrival. But it's not really that important, in my view, whether it was 1300 hours or 1500 hours. What is important is that the session was held and the decisions that were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Panic. We will not view the video any further. But Your Honours, I believe this is still MFI, this video. Or has it been admitted into evidence? Oh, it has, all right. Thank you. We will not view the video any further, but I will put to you the following: Another witness who was in the yard of Velepromet and at the cabinet session that day says it began about 1.00 p.m. Are you still saying it was in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was certainly earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Court, it's 4697 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that a witness says you were in the Velepromet yard when the members of the cabinet arrived, do you still abide by your statement or does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, excuse me for being so direct, but I would say that this witness is evading the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's 4703. If I tell you that you did not carry a notepad with you when you went to the cabinet session but that you took with you a notebook and file and a folder and this was also stated by a witness?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. I abide by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's 4562, line 18. Very well, Mr. Panic. If I tell you that some witnesses who are members of the cabinet told us that there was an informal meeting that day which began at 1400 hours at Velepromet and that no decision was taken there on handing over the prisoners. Those are Exhibits 387, pages 3145 to 3148; Exhibit 388, pages 3172 to 3191; Exhibit 389, pages 2507 and 2508, 2536 and 2537; and Exhibit 390, pages 3056 to 3071. What would you say to that? First of all, that it was not a session; secondly, that it began at 2.00 p.m.; and thirdly, that no decisions were made on handing over war prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the witness probably had some sort of interest, or witnesses, because they obviously circumvented the truth. I know where I was, and I know what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I put to you that with respect to the notebook that you showed here, you wrote those notes only later, whereas when you attended the cabinet session, you had a notebook with you in which you entered maybe official information about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I look like that sort of man to you? I have handed over a piece of material evidence. All I had was this little notepad in my pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you note down the conclusions of the session in that little notepad, since you made notes in it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't enter those conclusions so fast. I committed them to memory. What mattered to me at that time, and I didn't even have the patience to write it down, was that I couldn't understand the desire to make such a decision and that they wanted not only to put those people on trial, but also to bring back those who were already in Mitrovica. I simply remember that. It is engraved in my memory and will stay there for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You didn't note down that they decided the prison would be at Ovcara. You didn't note down what you said at that session; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't noted down. In that little notepad, I noted down only what I submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You didn't note down what Colonel Vujic said, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would have needed quite a lot of time to write that down. I didn't have time to take notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to make those notes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as each minister or each participant in the discussion took the floor, without even knowing who they were, I just managed to note down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If this was so, what sort of handover was it? Who was supposed to hand them over? Was it you? Were you given the task of handing them over?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, nor was I authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, who was tasked with handing over those people to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the problem. That's the issue that has to be proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But when this becomes evident, then the truth will be known about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was supposed to be no handover to anyone by our command. They were supposed to be screened, selected. The combatants were supposed to be separated off from the non-combatants, the patients, and the wounded, and they were to be transported to Sremska Mitrovica. Nowhere was anything said, by anyone, in anyone's presence, at the command post in the barracks, or anywhere else in the area at that time about their handing over to the civilian authorities. The problem of who handed them over is something that has to be proved and when this is proved, it will be easier to arrive at the truth about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, you didn't even know who handed them over, who was supposed to hand them over where or when this was supposed to take place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know only what I heard at the cabinet session, that they would put them on trial and that the prison would be at Ovcara. Who solved the technical issues, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they were solved at all? Did you ever see a document to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No document was ever drawn up, nor did I ever see one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the interpreters can hear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the notes you took in that little notepad?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were for my personal use, to be able to inform my commander if there was discussion of this, so I could give him specific details, and unfortunately, now it's being used to prove the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that a witness said that when you entered the cabinet session, you did not sit down, that you did not speak, but that the members of the cabinet immediately gathered around you and that the meeting was over - that's 4563 for the Court - what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that there was some ulterior motive behind saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that an officer who attended the cabinet session, whom you say you only met later on, told you on the 19th of November, before the cabinet session, or rather not told you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "But met you".

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you meet and get to know this man on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that he saw me. It's possible that he knew who I was. I was the Chief of Staff and I moved around quite a lot. If he was at the command post at any time, he could have seen me there, but I only got to know him later, later on. Even at that time, I did not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your notepad, why doesn't it say what Goran Hadzic said, or didn't he speak at the cabinet session?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't note down what Goran Hadzic said because I know him and logically, if he was the prime minister, he chaired the session and of course he spoke. We have video clips and we saw yesterday what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that, with respect to the cabinet session, in a previous case, he stated the following -- that's in the Dokmanovic case, page 3123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the witness testimony is being put from the other trial, I would not wish the transcript to be read out. Could the counsel give him the gist, because this is in line with the decision that was taken by the Chamber, not that I object really to having the transcript read out, but it's a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the point that's important, not the wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If he said at the meeting, "That prisoners of war are an issue for the JNA, that the JNA does not recognise their civilian courts and that civilian courts have no jurisdiction over these cases" and that that was all that was said about prisoners of war, do you remember this from the cabinet session?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not my words. Bogdan Vujic might have said that, Colonel Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I just paraphrased to you were the words of Goran Hadzic about this being uttered by some colonel or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Goran Hadzic probably said that to protect himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned an interview that he gave. When they asked him about the interview that you mention here that we saw on videotape here, he said, [In English] "Only for the purposes of the political marketing and in order to promote the government which did not have support among the people, and, if you noticed, my conclusion in the latter part was to ease the tensions and to have some kind of normalisation and to let people go, and I tried to prevent a possible euphoria among the people and I called up upon all to act with reserve." [Interpretation] So this is reference 3019 from the same transcript, Dokmanovic case. Do you believe -- 3109 is the transcript reference. Would you agree that this was a political position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a political position, but he adapted it to the needs of his defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the Ovcara case, in the Belgrade Ovcara case, on page 40 of B/C/S version, you said that the delegation of your unit went to see the Federal Secretary of National Defence in the morning on the 21st of November and that they went in a helicopter, one helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I remember I stated that and I can reiterate it now. Our delegation, which was supposed to meet with the Federal Secretary for National Defence, Army General Kadijevic, went on the 21st in the morning, I think it was around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that they went in one helicopter to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have said that. Most likely they flew in a helicopter. I can't remember now, but if I said helicopter, then that's how it must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that same statement, on page 58, did you state that that morning, the 21st of November, 1991, you signed an order on resubordinating these units, as deputy commander, in the absence of Mr. Mrksic. Did you state that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a document concerning that and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit 422.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this the document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I am putting to you Mr. Mrksic's position, that he wasn't in the helicopter which went on the 21st to Belgrade with the delegation, but rather that Major Tesic was in that helicopter and Mr. Mrksic had gone to Belgrade the night before with another colonel. Do you have any information concerning that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that. I stand by my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Panic. Tell me, please, this order here, you signed it at 6.00 on the 21st of November, 1991, pursuant to the order of the 1st Military District 115-151; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if this order 115-151, the same text is used as the one seen in your document such as Seselj's men, Sumadinac detachment and so on. Were such terms used in the order of the 1st Military District and was that the content that you simply transferred into your own document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These terms were not used in the order of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why were they then used in this document? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only possibility is that the author of this order, initials are RT, I suppose it stands for Radoje Trifunovic, who was an operations officer, that he was the one who added these terms and I accept that I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time when you signed it, did you read this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it and I signed it and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see document ERN 0D000343. And I have the English version here for everybody else. Could the usher please assist me. Could we now zoom in on the first portion of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, this is the document marked "strictly confidential 115-151"; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out the title of this document, of the heading?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Command of the 1st Military District, strictly confidential, 115-151." I think that the date is the 20th. It's not very legible in my copy. The 20th of November, 1991. And then it says, "Forward to," and then we see all of the units to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the text beneath it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information on results of combat activities at the Slavonia front forwarded by ..." So this document is entitled "Information."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you will agree with me that this is not an order but rather a document entitled "Information" issued by the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this document is the document that is referred to in your order signed on the 21st of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at another exhibit, please, 368.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, let's look at the heading of this document. First, "strictly confidential 467-1, 21st of November, 1991." Did you sign this? This is a combat report sent to the command of the 1st Military District and cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence. Did you sign this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down, please, to the portion where they discuss units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Mr. Panic, that in this report of yours sent to the command, you didn't write any of the things that you said had happened at the cabinet session, and that you testified about. Can we agree that it's not stated here that a decision was taken at the cabinet session to surrender prisoners, nor that somebody agreed to that, nor that these prisoners were handed over. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. This is dated the 21st, and as for these facts, if they were supposed to be conveyed to the 1st Military District, they were supposed -- it was supposed to be done on the 20th of November, because all reports are written for the previous 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this report of yours for the 20th of November at 1800 hours is something that you report on on the following day at -- in the morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the translation is correct. I went too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This report covers the period from 1800 hours on the 20th of November to 1800 hours of the 21st of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, just another issue that we need to clarify concerning your note, the notes you jotted down at the cabinet session. The date on the top is the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on this note, you refreshed your memory as you were preparing for various testimonies that you gave concerning dates and events that you testified about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, lately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about previously? Did you use it when giving your previous statements or was it the case that you just took it out now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I showed it before the military court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Correct, that was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you, then, explain -- do you remember whether you gave a statement to the security organ of the Guards Brigade in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a brief statement, one page long.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that statement, you said that the cabinet session took place in Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a major error. If that is what is recorded, then the date is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, is this the statement you gave to the security organ in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does it say in the first paragraph that the cabinet session was on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the date.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a major error.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you sign this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I was wrong, thinking that it was on the 19th, so the only mistake is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I have to tell you that our position is that you testified here the way you testified in order to shift responsibility for what happened at Ovcara between the 20th and the 21st of November when you served as commander in the absence of commander to my client, Mr. Mrksic, to shift responsibility to him and that there was no surrender whatsoever of prisoners to civilian authorities in Vukovar. This is our position. That can be seen in this statement that you gave where you failed to mention anything about Mrksic giving any suggestions about the surrender of prisoners. I'm now referring to the statement that you gave to security organs.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was an internal one and it was taken by the then Colonel Pero Kovacevic who served as security organ in the Guards Brigade. He did not participate in the Vukovar operation. He remained in Belgrade with the unit which remained to secure facilities and to provide security to persons. He asked me to tell him briefly about the cabinet session. I accept that I signed this and I reiterate that the only mistake is in the date. As for me shifting responsibility to anyone else, first of all, you are claiming that I am shifting responsibility to my commander, your client. I have a lot of respect for him and I repeat once again that he was a good commander with a lot of authority. He had full information about the events, and as such, we all held him in high esteem. As for my responsibility, I was Chief of Staff, and I was his deputy in his absence. I never wanted to evade my own responsibility. I'm not doing that now either. I can corroborate this by stating that I gave at least five various statements up to now. In various locations, at various points in time, I even went to Novi Sad, even though it wasn't strictly necessary for me to go there to give a statement. Otherwise, in talking to our officers and soldiers, participants of the events, I always emphasised that I wished to testify in order to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I hate to interrupt you, but you know that we are short of time. The Trial Chamber has given me the time it has.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a direct attack on my person and my liberty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's why I let you speak but I see that we are running out of time. With Their Honours leave, I will let you continue speaking. I may have overstepped the mark.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we are all doing that, but we are trying to arrive at the truth here. Even in the most difficult situations, I always went to testify. I have come here, and whether I am a witness for the Prosecution or for the Defence, or for the Defence of this or that person is immaterial to me. I was a person who was a participant in certain events. I remember what I can remember after the lapse of time, but I am someone who wants the truth to be established for the sake of all of us who carried out our tasks in an honourable manner, for the sake of those who were killed, for the sake of the victims in this war, and for the sake of a lesson to be learned by future generations. And I have nothing further to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have finished my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. As you will have noticed, the Chamber felt that the matters you were dealing with were sufficiently important to warrant you being allowed to continue. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: First you spoke about assault detachments. You said that they were of a temporary nature?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You even said until they had carried out their task. My question is the following: On the 18th of November, when Vukovar was liberated, what was the fate of the assault detachments as of that date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 18th of November, when Vukovar was liberated, the assault detachments no longer existed. There was no longer any need for them. Every unit went back to its establishment unit. The Territorial Defence unit was sent back to Velepromet, to its pre-war situation, and the battalions which, by the establishment, belonged to the Guards Brigade, went back to the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until the decision on resubordination was issued, which we saw on the screen, of the 21st, so from the 18th to the 21st of November, who controlled the Territorial Defence in Vukovar? Under whose control were they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the principles for the use of territorial units, they may be placed under the command -- well, that's what our rules and regulations say. They can be placed under the command of a JNA unit until a particular task is carried out. As the task was completed on the 18th, the TO units were no longer under the command of the JNA. And allow me to state my opinion. For practical reasons, these people were local people who had been born there, they had their homes there, their facilities, they had their own staff, and both they and we could hardly wait for them to return to their original situation before the combat operations began. That's why I assert that on the 18th, for all practical purposes, they ceased to be part of our troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we have a written order dated the 21st of November, and in your response you said that before this written order on resubordination to the 80th Kragujevac unit, first there was an oral order, then there's a comment, and it says written order to follow. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was talking about yesterday. An order can arrive in code, it can be issued by telephone, it can be oral or it can be written. Very often, because of the dynamic nature of events, an oral order would be issued first followed by a written order, and that's what happened in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If I were to tell you that a commander stated that on the 19th or the 20th, he received an oral order from Mrksic that he was no longer to have any contact with the Territorial Defence and that he passed this on to his company commanders, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it would be possible because all this can be conveyed in direct contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My question with respect to Ovcara is the following: As you came up to the hangar, opposite the entrance to the hangar, did you observe a big hole and did you see any corpses in that hole?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. That would certainly have attracted my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you tell us, in your estimation, how many people were milling around? I won't quote what you stated in the Belgrade municipality -- in the Belgrade Ovcara case?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was between 10 and 15 people, not more than 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As Chief of Staff, did you ever hear that in Nova Ulica, at the Miroslava Radic observation point was the Main Staff for the planning operation for the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't here hear that because we had a single command. That would have been a kind of shadow commander; it would have been duplicating the command. I simply never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was Nova Ulica a kind of command post where operations were planned?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's impossible. I don't know what that might have been. I never heard of it. What can I say? If someone mentions some kind of command post, a battalion commander can have a command post. That would be Borivoje Tesic on the left wing or, rather, on that axis. I was there at this command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there can only be an observation post or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you visit the unit where there were problems? Did you know whether there were any problems at the Miroslava Radica observation post on the axis of action of his troops?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of any problems with respect to Miroslav Radic, the company commander. What I know from that time, is that in that company, there was discipline. If I can say this, I still wonder why Miroslav Radic is on this list, how this came about, because he is a prototype of a guards officer and commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear anywhere and at the briefing in Negoslavci, was there any mention of Miroslav Radic having any kind of task relating to the evacuation of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And did you ever see, on the 19th or the 20th, Radic in the barracks and did he have any kind of tasks, to your knowledge, in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the barracks, it was the military police organs and units that had tasks. The 2nd Battalion, the 2nd Motorised Battalion was in the barracks and that was outside his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question: You were shown Exhibit 418 on the screen here. That is that order about place commanders, town commanders in Ovcara, and to avoid wasting time, it says that the town commander of Petrova Gora on the 19th of November, was Borivoje Tesic for Petrova Gora, and for the area from the cemetery to the Vuka River. My question is the following: As you have explained to Their Honours what powers the town commander had, if the Petrova Gora detachment and the Leva Supoderica detachment were in the area, which was under the control and command of the town commander, Borivoje Tesic, who would have control over them in a situation where they were doing something illegal, taking actions that were illegal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town commander received his tasks and authorisation and he was responsible for the area we dubbed "the town." In that area, it was the town commander who was responsible. In this case, it would be Commander Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that he had effective control over all the forces covered by the command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's mixing apples and oranges. One thing is a town commander who controls, who is basically the substitute for a civil government. This is an issue of effective control which is a legal issue as well as a military issue. They are two separate and distinct issues that have nothing to do with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Borovic. I didn't hear what you were saying or I haven't received an interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Borovic speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I said: I'm sorry, Mr. Weiner, but you are mixing up apples and oranges. The town command is not a civilian authority, it's a military authority with all the powers that the town commander has in wartime conditions. So it's you mixing up apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Borovic and Mr. Weiner, it's a case of pears. Please continue with your questioning, Mr. Borovic. The point you have made, Mr. Weiner, is one that is very adequately dealt with either in your cross-examination and/or in your final address. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Weiner, I was only joking, of course. I have a great respect for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What did you say, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town commander is responsible because when the order was issued designating the town commanders, their tasks were listed to ensure law and order, to prevent sabotage, to allow the population to live in the area, to regulate traffic, and to slowly create the conditions for the functioning of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But my question was: Did he have effective control over all the forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he must ensure control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may have another minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have shown a document to the witness and the Court, that's 0D00343 and I have omitted to tender it so far. It is the report of the 1st Military District on combat activities in the Slavonian theatre. May it be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the date of that report, Mr. Vasic? Is that the report of the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I think this is an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume, then, at maybe nearer to ten to that I am able to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you commence, Mr. Weiner, may I mention one brief matter, essentially for Mr. Borovic. The motion on behalf of your client with respect to the notebook of Witness P002 and his recall has not been supported with enough of the information which the Chamber detailed in its original order allowing you leave to bring this forward. If you look to paragraph 4 of the decision of the 30th of August, 2006, you will he see set out the information which the Chamber seeks to be able to determine whether recall of the witness is justified. It would be necessary for you to prepare and file further information setting out what is required by the order and I would suggest to do so by Tuesday of next week. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I meant by Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions. My name is Phil Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. Okay. Now the first group of questions that I'm going to ask you or the first group of areas of questions are going to concern general areas relating to some of the information that you've provided in your different statements. All right. Thank you. As a matter of background, Operation Group South had a number of local, territorial and volunteer units in it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And these units were subordinated or under the command and control of Operation Group South?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For example, the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora TOs were subordinated to Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you are also aware that volunteers from Serbia were arriving on a daily basis into Operations Group South's zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it applied more in the second part of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when these groups arrived, they weren't independent, they became part of Operation Group South or under the command of Operation Group South.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And some smaller groups of volunteers were allowed to stay together during the military operations, but the larger groups were divided between the various JNA and TO units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not allow for a larger group of volunteers to exist because we didn't know their capabilities, so this is why we split them into several units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just briefly, you were aware that the Leva Supoderica detachment was recruited or sponsored by the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that after the operation, yes. I realised what the nature of that unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that that party was Seselj's party.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you also know that the front line units were a mixture of Guards Motorised Brigade units and local TO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that the combat readiness and operational strength of the local TO units and the volunteer units were much lower than that of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, even where those units, those TO or volunteer units were strongest, such as the reconnaissance of Vukovar, they still were not as good as the Guards Motorised Brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units of local TOs such as Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica, they were recruited from local people from the area who had their houses there, who knew Vukovar well, knew the streets, knew where barricades were, knew where paramilitary formations were setting up their defence. So in that respect, they provided a great deal of useful information to us. We used them in other assault detachments as scouts or guides when going on mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But would you agree that they still were not as good as the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified at the beginning that the Guards Motorised Brigade had two battalions of military police.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that there were hundreds of police officers or members within these battalions of military police?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in fact, in one of those units or battalions, they even had an anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that these units of military police were well-equipped and well-trained.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know that the Guards Motorised Brigade had two infantry battalions and an armoured battalion in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So would you agree, sir, that on November 20th, the Operational Group South or Guards Motorised Brigade had sufficient resources to neutralise or eliminate a threat to the prisoners by a group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as you said in your statement, the local Serbian TO was no match for the Guards Motorised Brigade. That's your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A few more general areas. You were not aware of any functioning civil or civilian police force while you were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were not aware of any functioning civil service while you were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was something that functioned in Negoslavci on a minor scale and also in some areas where there was no combat. As for authorities, the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Srem, it functioned but it was outside of our area of responsibility. I believe that at the time, they were -- they had their seat in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Within Vukovar, you were not aware of any functioning civil service within the town or city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had never seen any functioning judicial bodies in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during the conflict, that SAO government played no role in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know from my level, and I was just a Lieutenant Colonel at the time and Chief of Staff, I'm not aware of any role.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you indicated in previous statements that they were nowhere to be found; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never received any order from any higher command to recognise that government, that Serbian autonomous government.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were under no orders from the 1st Military District to abide by that government's decisions.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you stated that the Serbian autonomous or SAO government, Serbian autonomous government, had no actual authority and could not be considered a serious institution, at paragraph 71 of your ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. At the session itself, once their debate started, things looked quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But even though they made certain claims to have all of these functioning organs, you had never seen any of those.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the security organ of OG South never did an inquiry to see if they existed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue on with a few more general subjects. In your statement to the ICTY, you mentioned Major Sljivancanin, and you indicated that he liked to be the centre of attention; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to all of his qualities, one of his faults is that he wanted to have a high profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he liked to be on television and in the press a lot, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that Major Sljivancanin went well beyond what was required of him by his job description; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But please allow me to say this, that he did that with the best of intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that Major Sljivancanin - excuse me - did not limit his activities to what would be suspected of the head of a security organ, or security service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a person who was assistant commander for moral guidance, and he, who was supposed to be at the front line frequently to spend time with the troops for some reasons, and I don't want to judge anyone harshly, for some reasons, he failed to do that at the time. So part of those tasks related to moral guidance were carried out by Major Sljivancanin. He was the one who affected the morale of the troops by his presence, by his explanations, and by encouraging them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you also know, sir, that Major Sljivancanin did things that he wasn't supposed to do; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did more than necessary. He should have refrained and stuck to his security tasks, but allow me -- by spending time at the front line, he also did his work from the -- security-type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But he also did the work of others which he wasn't supposed to do. For example, at the briefings, he would be discussing the logistical needs of the Territorial Defence units which was not his responsibility; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did that with the intention to emphasise the needs that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But that wasn't his job. There was an assistant commander for logistics in OG South; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but the assistant commander for logistics should have spent more time in locations where Major Sljivancanin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, he would also discuss the needs of the 1st Assault Detachment even though that was Major Tesic's responsibility; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is within the framework of the local TO. Since they had poor weaponry and required ammunition as well as some other equipment that was lacking in the TO, he emphasised that, regardless of the presence of Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, sir, that was Major Tesic's responsibility and in your own words, that was an interference with Major Tesic's responsibility; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know that on his own initiative, he was out firing 60-millimetre mortars; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that Major Sljivancanin also corrected artillery fire in the Mitnica section; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But please allow me. As I was preparing for my testimony, I found some documents and I clarified certain issues for myself as to why he had done that. I am now convinced, and it can be corroborated by entries in the war diary, that he did that first and foremost for security reasons, in order to protect the lives of our people, because there was some doubt about the failings of our artillery. It's a serious problem, and sometimes that happens at the front, at the training polygon and even in peacetime and it affects adversely subordinated units. And it was both a command issue and a security issue and it is in this light that I interpret his involvement on that day because he was personally present there as it was taking place. Subsequently, after his intervention, it was established that there had been mistakes and, as I read in the entry, what caused these mistakes was that the gunpowder was humid and this is why they failed to reach targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You knew that Major Sljivancanin was not a person who'd be at the front lines correcting artillery fire. You knew he is not trained for that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but he didn't do that on his own; chief of artillery was with him as they corrected the mistake. He identified that. He asked the chief of artillery to go with him, and it is his mistake that he reported about that. He reported the superior command about that. It should have been done by the chief of artillery, he should have reported about the mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, he demanded that Zivota Panic, General Zivota Panic, be informed that he, Major Sljivancanin, was correcting artillery fire; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he even had that placed in the war diary; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Recorded, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that information relating to basic corrections of artillery fire do not mention or do not deserve being mentioned in a war diary; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was relevant because it affected adversely the morale of the troops because there were rumours circulating about that it wasn't just the paramilitary formations that were firing upon us but that we also came under friendly fire of our own artillery that was falling short of the mark. And I think that it was good that it was recorded in the war diary. I wish we had recorded more because it would have made the position of all of us easier now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, you know there's no indication in the diary, which is Exhibit 401 in this case, that there was any problem relating to friendly fire, that there was any problem relating to wet powder, that there was any problem relating to ill-precise firing; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in fact, as an assistant commander for the security, he should have notified his own commander, Colonel Mrksic, and not gone over Colonel Mrksic's head to Zivota Panic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know why this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you also discuss, in relation to Major Sljivancanin, that he had an argument with a ICRC, a Red Cross representative; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from the media. I know that that was immediately prior to the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that there was an impression shared by many that the ICRC's role was to save Croatian criminals; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more than one evacuation. I think there were two in October. We respected the cease-fire. The ICRC came to the hospital. They took the patients that the then director of the hospital, Vesna Bosanac, had prepared for the convoy, and they passed through our area of responsibility. Later on, we heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that next, but the question is first -- we'll get to that. There was an impression that was shared by many that the ICRC's role was to save Croatian criminals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To continue what I was saying, we heard that a large number -- that's why --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's okay. And I just want to ask you first that question. Number two, did Major Sljivancanin and yourself share that view?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to believe that some fighters had left with that convoy, but generally speaking, I wouldn't say that they were taking their side, they were doing their job. But I'm sure they were tricked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did Major Sljivancanin share the view that the ICRC's role was to protect or to save Croatian criminals, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't assert that now. I can't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you do know, sir, and you've indicated in your statement, that Major Sljivancanin was upset over reports that Croatian soldiers were able to escape during those prior evacuations which you had mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you also know that in October or sometime around October, Major Sljivancanin was very upset over his driver being killed in an ambush by Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a very difficult situation. Major Sljivancanin could also have been killed. He happened to stay alive and the man next to him, the driver, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was upset not only about, as you said, that his driver being killed, that he was almost killed himself in that ambush by Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to show you two photographs. They're both marked for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown MFI 198, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. In the red circle, that's Vojislav Seselj. On the right-hand side of the photograph, I recognise Major Tesic. I don't recognise the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be received as Exhibit 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, before I show you the next photograph, do you recall a man by the name of Lancuzanin, nicknamed Kameni?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Leva Supoderica Territorial Defence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown MFI 689, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see the picture on the top?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I recognise Major Sljivancanin, but not the other two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a man by the name of Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic -- well, I saw him there on several occasions. I think he wore a black hat. And I think he belonged to the Leva Supoderica Detachment. He was a local man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you describe his appearance, facial appearance?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he wore a beard when I saw him. And I saw him at the special court when I was asked whether I recognised any of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, can you look at that picture and do you recognise either of the men to the left or right of Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't. If the photograph were clearer, but I don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was leading by Mr. Weiner. The witness has already responded so there is no further need for me to object. I don't know whether counsel will put further questions on this document so I will wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your point is well made though. Carry on, Mr. Weiner, and be more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll leave that as an MFI, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified on Monday -- I'm sorry, on Wednesday, that when you got to the hospital, there were a number of corpses or dead bodies outside of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Across the road from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You described this sight in Belgrade at page 26 of your testimony as a distressing sight; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every normal person, when he sees a pile of corpses, would be upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you heard, outside the hospital, that those dead persons had been summarily tried and executed by the persons who were taking shelter in the hospital; isn't that what you testified to in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various comments about this going round, but the comment one could hear most frequently was that most of those corpses were people who had been in the hospital and had either died there, or when the paramilitaries escaped the hospital, they created room for themselves by ejecting those people. Those were the comments one could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In your statement on the 28th of December, you indicated that you believed that those -- that these were victims, these were Serbian victims who were killed and were thrown into the street. Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a belief that most of those people were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were even family members trying to identify these persons who they believed to be -- to have been summarily tried and executed by persons from the hospital. Do you recall that testimony before the Belgrade court?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some people who tried to recognise or identify some of the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you or any member of the JNA say to these people: Let's not get carried away. Let's not start on rumours. This might not be true. Did anyone try and quell those rumours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. There were several officers there and not I personally, I stayed there briefly, but those other officers intervened to prevent anyone coming there uninvited and saying that the process of identification remained to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
