utterances.text: That's the process of identification, but did you or anyone intervene and say: Let's not run off with these wild rumours. Let's everyone stay calm. Did you or anyone else say that to these people who were upset?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we all said that. I and everyone else who was there. People, we have more urgent business to deal with now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You just indicated that you did not say that personally on line 1 and 2 on page 45 of today's transcript. You've never previously testified that you ever tried to calm this situation out -- situation that occurred out in front of the hospital. Are you now saying you did?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't exert any special influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've never said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps the witness should first have been asked whether anyone put this question to him about attempts to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure you will be able to do that in re-examination, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've never stated in any previous statement or testimony that you've given since 1998 that anyone ever attempted to calm these people down. In fact, you personally believed that these victims were Serbs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody insisted on this. I was talking about other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you believe that these people were murdered Serbs and had been murdered by those in the hospital. That's what you've previously stated.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believed most of those people were Serbs. That was the information we had. And we accepted it at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was information from the people that were gathering outside the hospital, the local people.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from individuals who happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One more brief area and then we'll get to the main issues. You testified yesterday that the artillery would not have fired on water wells or people getting water. Remember that testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. And this is something I've heard here for the first time. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that seven or eight witnesses have testified in this case that the wells and the persons going for water were targeted in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were also aware, sir, that the JNA or local infantry units had mortars.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Petrova Gora TO had a mortar unit which was part of the 3rd Assault Group of the 1st Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So did you ever visit any of the mortar groups within the 3rd Assault Group of the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that on one or two occasions, I visited the 1st Assault Detachment and went up to the command post of Major Tesic. I did not tour any mortar crews specially, except for the official artillery groups of higher calibres which were behind Negoslavci, the 102-millimetre mortars which belonged to the 1st and 2nd Battalion. I did not, however, visit the smaller groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that mortars can be used to target moveable or stationary objects?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars are used to target, first of all, immoveable objects. With respect to moveable objects, only barrage fire can be carried out where live targets are expected to advance. A mortar is a weapon that cannot quickly change its settings and follow a moving target. So nowhere in the rules does it say that it's intended to fire on moveable objects. With respect to moveable targets, it can only be used for barrage fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A mortar can be used to fire upon a tank; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be used, but to no effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you know a mortar can be used to fire on human beings.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If they are in a group and if they are a stationary target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if you have a cluster of human beings getting water out of a well, a mortar could be used to fire upon that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And we also know that a well is obviously a stationary object which can be fired upon by mortars?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can, but a well is such a small target that there's little chance of hitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you weren't out with the small mortar groups, so you can't tell what they were doing or what they were hitting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. It would be guesswork on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the last few days about being ordered by Colonel Mrksic to attend a meeting at Velepromet. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there was an issue raised today as to whether or not -- or what exactly he told you in relation to the issue of their requests for prisoners. So my first question is: As best as you can recall, what did he tell you in relation to that request? Because you asked him: What do I say if they raise that issue? Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the 20th when the session was held. When I received the order or, rather, when the order was conveyed to me that I should report to Colonel Mrksic, I called him up by telephone and was given the following task by him: Go to Velepromet, to the cabinet session there. Convey my greetings to them, and tell them I am prevented from attending the session. I added to this or, rather, I responded: Is there any need for me to say something and what if there is a discussion about handing over the people in the hospital to the civilian authorities? Because I already had received information that they would be asking for this, that they would be asking that they be the ones to put them on trial. "Tell them I will accept the decision they make."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you said: "Tell them I will accept the decision they make," who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the words of my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You then went to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated previously in another statement, 2003, that the atmosphere was unpleasant. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That the army was being attacked in ugly terms.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That certain so-called representatives or representatives of so-called government said that they would prevent the army from transporting prisoners to the military facility at Sremska Mitrovica. Didn't that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there was a delegation of officials who came from outside of Vukovar to that meeting: Hadzic, Arkan and so on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most members of the delegation were from outside because this cabinet came from Dalj and I think that most of them were from outside of Vukovar. There were perhaps one or two from Vukovar, Bugunovic, and I can't remember the other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And within that delegation was Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time I had seen him in the flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you knew who Arkan was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew from the media who he was before he arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you testified yesterday at page 14376, that if he had arrived and was not in that delegation, you would have arrested him if he had tried to enter Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Had he arrived in any other manner, rather than with the delegation, especially while combat was still going on, he would have been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you know a few days prior to this meeting, you recall receiving a warning order, if you want to call it that, from General Panic, Zivota Panic, that some units, some TO units had already perpetrated acts of revenge. You remember that order or do you need to see it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that order arrived and it was written on the basis of some events in other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, my question to you, sir, is: Based on that warning, and what you saw and heard at that meeting, including the presence of Arkan, did you stop and contact Colonel Mrksic and advise him that there's a dangerous situation and he should reconsider or he must reconsider his decision? Did you take that action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff, I did nothing special except that we discussed it at the command post and that oral warnings were issued at every briefing and in personal contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were told by Colonel Mrksic basically before you went to the meeting: Let it be as that cabinet decides. When you got to that meeting and you saw the ugly situation, and you saw Arkan sitting there as a member of that government or a delegate from that so-called government, and also knowing of that warning from Zivota Panic, when you see this situation happening, did you leave the meeting and contact Colonel Mrksic and say to him: There's a dangerous situation here. I think you better reconsider your decision. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. It would have been better if I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact -- may the witness please be shown the law on service in the armed forces, Exhibit 583, please. I'm sorry, 584, please. Exhibit 584. It's 00364339 to 00364395. Now, could we go to Article 53. In the English, it's on page 28. In the B/C/S, it's on page 00364344. No, no, go down a little bit. Article 53. Or go up, I'm sorry. Stop right there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the first sentence of that indicates that: "Members of armed forces shall be duty-bound to carry out orders issued by their superior officers, while their superior officers are in the execution of their office, unless it is clear that carrying out such orders would constitute a criminal offence."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, based on what you had seen at that meeting, and what had happened at the barracks earlier there, where people were trying to get to the buses, just before the meeting, and based on the warning from Zivota Panic, did you refuse to carry out that order knowing that it would result in a crime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing indicated that there would be a crime committed here. I attended a cabinet session pursuant to my orders. There was another officer there, a colonel. I didn't know who he was, and pursuant to his orders, he was there or what his powers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, in your own statement, you've indicated that they were attacking the colonel, that people were indicating they would disobey the orders of the army. You had seen them attempting to attack the buses earlier that morning. You were aware of acts of retribution or revenge. At that point, it was foreseeable that something bad was going to happen, especially with seeing Arkan there as part of this so-called government delegation; Arkan, a person who kills for fun. Did you at that point either contact Colonel Mrksic and ask him to reconsider or did you, at that time, refuse to implement that order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't contact Colonel Mrksic. Again, I listened to their debate, and at one point I conveyed to them the position of Mrksic, that he would accept the decision they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 77 of your statement to the OTP, you said that you were tricked into attending this meeting. Did you say that because you realise that you were sent to deliver an order that was wrong and would foreseeably result in a crime occurring?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was surprised that I was sent to the cabinet session. That had not been discussed previously. But I also cannot doubt my commander believing that he had sent me to that session to entrap me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm objecting, because in paragraph 77 of the statement of this witness, I don't see what Mr. Weiner put to him, that he was trapped into going to this session. I think it would be proper to put the exact words to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The word "tricked" was used. I will read the paragraph. Could we go to 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Second last line, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a copy of your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor? It was given to you yesterday. We'll give you another copy if you need one. If you could turn to paragraph 77 on page 20.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it. It is possible that this was not an ideal translation. Perhaps it should be clarified. I'm reiterating that I cannot believe that I was sent there with any bad intentions. That was the sense of my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you said you were tricked into being sent there; isn't that correct? That's the word you used "tricked"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a correct interpretation. I was ordered to go. And in my reasoning, I simply cannot allow myself to believe that I had been sent there on purpose, that they wanted to sacrifice me. That's the essence of what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But even without their intention, sir, once you arrived at that meeting and saw what was happening, and had seen what was happening during that day, and saw the situation, and being aware of Zivota Panic's warning, you had a duty to disobey that order or contact General -- I'm sorry, Colonel Mrksic, and have him reconsider that decision and you didn't do that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask for him to reconsider. He had assessments, both from the cabinet session, from the hospital, and from Velepromet, about the situations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you had assessments on the ground. You had just seen an incident at the barracks where local TO members were trying to get at the people on the buses. You had just seen Arkan as being part of this so-called government's delegation. You had heard the statements attacking the JNA at this meeting. Did you, at that point, notify Colonel Mrksic and say: "We've got a serious problem here. Someone's going to be killed"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not conclude that somebody would be killed, but upon my return to the barracks, I informed Colonel Mrksic briefly about the cabinet session and their decision. And I went back to my other duties. There was nothing to hint that it would end in this way except for a heated debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, there was more than a heated debate and you had already had observations of TO members attempting to attack the bus with people in it and it was only because of your military police that they didn't enter it, according to your testimony. You even said, if we go to paragraph 71, that this wasn't a normal hand-over. You knew there was something wrong. You knew that this wasn't a normal hand-over. If you could turn to paragraph 71 which is on page 18 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S. I'll read it: "The order of the 1st Military District referred to above does not include the hand-over of evacuated individuals to the civilian authorities of the SAO SBZS. I do not recall a single document ordering the hand-over of evacuated individuals to the civilian authorities of the SAO SBZS. In retrospect, I have to say that such a hand-over was not normal since the SAO SBZS government had no actual authority and therefore, could not be considered a serious institution." That's what you said, isn't that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew the situation was not normal.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not normal. The situation was not normal, just as the war is not a normal social phenomenon. But that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, there is no mention in the war diary of that hand-over, is there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we look at page 94 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 94 - excuse me - on page 25. Let me read it and you can follow along. I will read your statement. "In the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade, ERN B/C/S 0293-5434-0293-5482, ERN English L0100496-L0100537. War diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade for the period from 1st October until 22nd November, 1991." "There is no record of the hand-over of prisoners from the hospital to local Serbian authorities. This is an omission. The hand-over was an important event and should have been recorded in the war diary. Regular combat reports of OG South for the 21st, ERN B/C/S 0327-1248-0327-1248. English, ET03271248-0327-1248, and the 22nd November, ERN B/C/S 0327-1249, 0327-1249. English ET, 0327-1249-0327-1249 also show no mention of the hand-over. Since the hand-over took place on the 20th, it should have been included in the report of the 20th although I can see that the reports of the 21st and the 22nd also mentioned evacuations that took place on the 20th." Do you agree that's what it says there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And those are your words?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell us, why wasn't the notation placed in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated previously and I can repeat it, I believe this to be an omission, a mistake, and I think that it came about because the combat had been over and there needed to be more supervision over the work of the officer entering data.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Major Trifunovic was a very careful person; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's not the type of person to omit significant details, is he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was considered to be a responsible operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And not only is this important event, and that's how you describe it, important event not described in the war diary, it's not described in any report from the Guards Motorised Brigade or Operations Group South; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular event is not described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that was purposely omitted for reasons of criminal liability? That's why it wasn't listed in any of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. I think this to be an omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it's an omission not just in the war diary, but all of the combat reports that were filed after November 20th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to continue. Is this the time for the break or is it another five or ten minutes or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be normally ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From the barracks -- I'm sorry, you returned to the barracks after this meeting, and you notified General Mrksic of the results. From there --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From there, you went to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went back to the barracks immediately after the cabinet session. I called Commander Mrksic. I informed him about the cabinet session and their decision, told him briefly about the situation, saying that there was a colonel there, whose name I later learned, but I never knew, pursuant to his orders, and for what reason he attended the session. I do not know this to this day. Following that, I continued with my work, together with other organs of command to prepare the press conference that was to be held on the following day. That lasted until the afternoon hours. It was only in the afternoon that I went to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what I meant, sir. From there, meaning from the barracks, you went to Ovcara. Now, yesterday, you testified --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified at page 14324: "I felt it necessary to see whether these people from the hospital were actually put up at Ovcara, to see whether the -- or there are authorities that made a decision at the -- it's just -- not properly written -- to see whether the authorities that made a decision at the session and concluded that they would be running a trial, to see whether they actually arrived on the spot and quite simply, what was going on at Ovcara, so that when arriving at the command post, I'd give more complete information about that to the commander." Do you recall that testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. I went there to see whether the organs of authorities had arrived and whether they started with trials, not whether there was anything going on pursuant to the decision they had made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No one ordered you to go there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one did. I believed that I needed to be fully informed, so that once I come to the command post, I could inform the commander about it. And I am repeating for the umpteenth time that I was truly convinced, having heard their debate and how they had all organs of authorities and even courts of two instances, which is something that Goran Hadzic had stated, I was convinced that they would be able to give these people a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you used the words yesterday at page 14324: "I felt it necessary." That phrase right there, "I felt it necessary," in relation to you going to Ovcara. You're very careful with your language, sir. You were worried about your liability over carrying out Colonel Mrksic's orders and that a crime would occur. That's why you felt it was necessary to go to Ovcara; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, let me tell you. I wasn't worried about myself, not in the least. In that unfortunate town of Vukovar, those who were alive frequently envied the dead. My life did not exist as such. It was the lives of our soldiers and people who shared the same fate that existed. At that moment in time, I did not think about myself and my own responsibility. What I thought about was how they were going to implement what they had decided, and I needed to see what was going on in order to be able to inform the commander. I'm telling you this sincerely, as a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said you felt it was necessary to go there. You went out of your way and went there. And you did that because you were worried or concerned that something bad was going to happen. You had already seen what had occurred during the day; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered the question that Mr. Weiner is repeating for the second time, probably because he wasn't happy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, it's not harassing at this point, so it may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll read the question again, sir: "You said, you felt it necessary to go there. You went out of your way and went there. And you did that because you were worried or concerned that something bad was going to happen. You had already seen what had occurred that day; isn't that correct?"

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason was to see whether they had arrived on the spot and whether they started with trials and I needed to see that in order to be able to inform the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You further testified, sir, on pages 14324, that you went to Ovcara or you decided to stop at Ovcara which was on the road between the barracks and the command post. It was along the roadway between the barracks and the command post. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 156, please. It's a map of the area. Could you reduce it, please, so you can see Ovcara and the command post. Could you focus a little bit on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we have these pens where you can write on the map. The first question is: Do you recognise that area? Could you put a one, please, next to the barracks where you were.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And let's go down. Could you put a 2 next to where the command post was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you put a 3 next to Ovcara where you went.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that Ovcara is not along the roadway between the barracks and Negoslavci, or is this map incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a correct map, and I didn't say that it was right on the road. I said it was en route from the barracks to Negoslavci. Travelling on the road, I turned to the left and I stopped by Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, why don't you draw a line from the barracks and show us the route that you went to Ovcara, and then the route that you returned. First, the route that you went from the barracks to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you put an A next to that, somewhere along the line, so we know that that's the first route. A letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's good. Thank you. And sir, could you put a line and show us the route of how you returned to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same, except in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you put a B by the arrow or the arrowtip so we know that's the second route from Ovcara to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honour, is it time for the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you tendering that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I thought I will do it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can lose it electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 854, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then adjourn and resume at ten to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I start, both counsel, Mr. Lukic and Mr. Moore, have requested to address the Court in the five minutes before the session ends today, at 20 minutes to 2.00, concerning the programme for the briefs, getting the briefs and the argument, oral argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will let you off the hook a little earlier, Mr. Weiner. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Sir, as you can see on the map in front of you, Ovcara is not along the road between the barracks and the command post. As you testified yesterday, it was necessary for you to go there and I put it to you you took that detour because you were concerned that a crime was going to occur at Ovcara based on your conveying the orders of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this. I have already said, returning to the command post on my way back, I wanted to see whether some kind of investigative or other judicial proceeding had started because they had announced that such a thing would happen at the cabinet session. Ovcara is not on the main road, but it's on the way from Vukovar to Negoslavci, it's in that direction. So only a brief detour was needed; I only had to turn left at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You wanted to see if any trial or judicial process had started because you were worried, having seen that so-called government meeting, who you had never seen before, and seeing Arkan there, that it all might be a fraud and a crime would be occurring or something very bad would be happening.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have the remotest idea that something bad would happen. I just wanted to have complete information about what was happening and to inform my commander of it. At the cabinet session, they spoke very convincingly about holding a fair trial. Hadzic said that those who had bloodied their hands would be put on trial, whereas those who were innocent would remain living in Vukovar in a normal way. I could not gather that they were preparing for anything else. I thought that, as a government, they were competent because that's how they represented themselves. I thought they were competent to do things properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you'd never seen them before. You didn't know anything about them, and the member of the delegation that you did know about was a criminal and a murderer. You didn't look into it, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you've already previously testified that you didn't -- I'm sorry, you testified, I'm talking back in Belgrade -- that you didn't know who ordered those buses to go from the barracks to Ovcara; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the questions that needs resolving.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that military police were escorting them to Ovcara but you didn't know exactly from which military police battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the police of the 2nd Battalion of the military police together with the unit that had secured them in the barracks, the unit of Captain Predojevic who were escorting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you knew who were escorting them, but you did not know who ordered them there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know now. I learned later on, because later on, I saw who was escorting them and I learned the details later on. But I did not see the convoy setting out from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you learned later on that they were sent -- that they were escorted by the military police to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you said you went to Ovcara, and I want to quote you, "so you would have complete information." You didn't have complete information about why those people left the barracks but you wanted complete information as to what was going on in Ovcara? If you wanted complete information, you should have gone back to the command post and said: What is going on here? Shouldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have done that, but I went first to Ovcara and then to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you went to Ovcara and -- what did you see when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at Ovcara, I saw a hangar and guards in front of the hangar. On the road in front of the hangar, I saw several armed men, and I also believe there were individuals without weapons. It was not a large group of people, maybe 10 to 15 on the road. Some were circulating. They may have been carrying out a task and just passing through, but most of the group hung around. One of them tried to approach the gate to the hangar but they were prevented by the guards, that is, the military police unit standing guard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there's been testimony here, that's uncontested from both military and civilian witnesses, that when those buses arrived at Ovcara, the prisoners had to run through a gauntlet to get to the hangars where they were beaten with fists, beaten with feet, and beaten with metal and wooden objects. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that later on in my conversation with Vujnovic but not described so dramatically. I just learned that there was some attempts to assault those people and some people were continuing trying to approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that, your conversation, shortly. But were you aware of the gauntlet, sir, and people were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some of this from Vojnovic and I learned some of this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There has been testimony that a few members of the Guards Motorised Brigade, including an officer, participated in the gauntlet; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know if there was anyone there before I arrived. I did not participate in that. I can assert that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There has been testimony in this court, sir, that you were present and were watching the gauntlet as it was conducted and the prisoners were being beaten. Do you deny this? And that's testimony at page 7705 and 7706.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny that testimony. I would not have been able to observe that. I would have prevented it. I would have opposed it physically, because it's neither good for a soldier or a human being to do something like that. I arrived when these people were already in the hangar. And yesterday, I explained that at that time, the buses were turning on the road behind Ovcara in the direction of Grabovo and going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There has been testimony that the military police officers who you saw on those buses, and the drivers, took no action to protect those prisoners as they were beaten, as they ran through the gauntlet. Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that or, rather, I saw that there were two policemen on each bus plus a driver. At that point, they were on the way back to the barracks. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Colonel Vojnovic attempted to protect the prisoners that were entering the hangar? Colonel Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vojnovic told me that. He told me about the attempt or, rather, the gauntlet at the entrance to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's testified that he was pushed, struck, or assaulted, and harassed as he helped save some of those prisoners. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the story he told me was not so miserable. He was a soldier, an officer. We did agree together that the security had to be reinforced. So it's his own fault if he was pushed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 67, in the reply, line 12, the witness said he, meaning Vojnovic, was the commander and he had his military police. This is not on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have spoken very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer? The question was: "He testified," meaning Colonel Vojnovic, of the 80th Motorised Brigade, "He testified that he was pushed, struck or assaulted, and harassed as he helped save some of those prisoners. Were you aware of that?" Could you please repeat your answer. It did not come through on the record.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojnovic told me that he had certain problems when these people got off the buses and proceeded to the hangar. He said that they created a gauntlet and tried to settle accounts with them. He did not tell me what they had done to him. I say that if they pushed him around, harassed him, threatened him, dragged him around, he, himself, was to blame because he was a commander who had a military police unit there and other units he could have used for his own personal protection and for the protection of other persons who were under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that he's to blame for acting heroically and saving people? He's to blame for getting pushed and injured or hurt?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't what I meant to say. I meant to say that he, as a commander, should not allow himself to be in a situation where he is not protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, you just testified that if you were there - you claim that you weren't there when the gauntlet - and if you were there, you would have gone right in to protect those people. He did the same thing as you would have done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't his fault. It was a heroic gesture, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that but I would have done it more professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, he also described the scene in the hangar of those people who'd been beaten and he described it at page 8844 as a "shocking sight." You saw the people in that hangar who had been beaten. Did you also see this shocking sight?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the people from the entrance to the hangar, from the gate. I didn't go in. And in the hangar, nothing was happening at that point, except for people standing around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you spoke to Colonel Vojnovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And yesterday, you testified at page 14325 about that conversation. "We exchanged a few words and he told me that there had been attempts made for those who were in front of the hangar and on the road or, rather, by them to enter the hangar and recognise someone. Quite simply, he said to me, that he had the impression that some people were trying to take revenge, wanted to take revenge, but that he did not allow that, and that his security did not allow that, the security that was in front of the hangar." Is that what you testified to yesterday as to the conversation that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Today, you're testifying that he advised you that there was a gauntlet. You know what a gauntlet is. That's different -- you know what a gauntlet -- that's different from an impression that some people were trying to take revenge. That's a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very well. I may not have been sufficiently precise yesterday. I may not have stated all the information, but if need be, I can go into great detail when describing an event. Yesterday, I was trying to be brief, as I am today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, a gauntlet where people are being beaten, especially prisoners, is a very serious situation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What, exactly, did he describe to you in relation to this gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have to go into details. When the people got off the buses and as I have been there, I know the distance is not great, it's just 7 or 800 meters from the road to the hangar, it's a path going up. He did not go into details, but he said that when the people were getting off the buses, those people gathered around trying to identify individuals and they stood on both sides, so they did, in fact, create some kind of gauntlet. He said he was there and that he intervened personally and prevented it. He said that he had some problems, that the situation was now quiet, calm, which I could see for myself, and that was it. We concluded together that security had to be reinforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The gauntlet you described was some sort of identification gauntlet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Vojnovic could explain it better than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, his explanation was a gauntlet where people were being beaten with fists, feet, metal, and wooden objects. That's much more serious than an identification gauntlet of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he had just gone through this serious situation where he threw himself into this to protect people, this had just occurred, and are you telling us that he never described it to you or told you what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke in front of the hangar, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you want to leave it that all he told you was that it was his impression that some people wanted to take revenge?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put to briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true, that he told you about the serious threat to the prisoners and that's why you went back to notify Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there, the situation was under control. Security at the entrance to the hangar, in the hangar, people who were not being beaten up at that point in time by anyone and nobody was doing anything to them at that time. People on the road were milling around. Some were stopping to look. Others were trying to approach the hangar. In front of the hangar, there was Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. After my conversation with him and after what I had seen, I went back to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said after what you had seen. He described the people in the hangar after being beaten as a shocking situation. You looked into that hangar and as I said, it's been uncontested here that this gauntlet occurred and beatings, what did you see? You didn't see any people bleeding? You didn't see any people who were injured?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter the hangar, and I was unable to see individual faces. I saw a large group of people standing. The hangar was half-lit. It had no proper windows, just tiny ones, and the light came in through tiny cracks. I couldn't see the faces clearly, I just saw a crowd of people standing. They stood further away from the door, opposite at quite far from the door. I didn't enter the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said you went to Ovcara to get a complete picture of what was happening. You didn't go into the hangar to get that complete picture of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter the hangar. I was primarily interested in finding out whether the government, which had promised a fair trial, had arrived and started with a trial, whether they started taking records or doing something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if we look at the date so far, you've been to the barracks in the morning and there was an incident at the barracks where TO people were trying to attack the people on the bus and the military police had to stop them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You attend a meeting where Arkan is on the government delegation, where they are attacking the JNA, indicating they will not obey the orders of the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, but I don't see on the basis of what he put before the witness that Arkan was a member of the government delegation. No witness stated that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was his testimony yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I recall evidence, Mr. Vasic, that Arkan arrived as a member of the government delegation and accompanying Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, you're aware, from a few days earlier, a warning from General Zivota Panic of TO members taking revenge and your testimony in its best light is that Colonel Vojnovic indicated that some local people wanted to take revenge; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At that point, sir, you knew that there was a serious problem, a serious threat to these prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I also knew that nothing could happen to them if we intervened with our forces and that was never in question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that in a little bit. You left Ovcara knowing that there was a serious threat, and you returned to your command post and spoke with Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified that you spoke to Colonel Mrksic about what you knew, and that's at page 14328 to 14329. And I'll read what you testified yesterday. "I informed him about all of this. I said it wouldn't be a bad thing if some of the security organs or military police went to Ovcara to indicate certain things or offer assistance in professional terms, if necessary, to Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. I don't know whether he sent anyone. I think he did, and think on the basis of everything I remember, and having made these previous statements too. I think that he actually did send some people there and I think that Mile Bozic was among them. He was there in Negoslavci at the command post or, rather, in a house there near the command post." That was your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that testimony was not totally correct or accurate or true, whichever word you want to use?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you notified Colonel Mrksic in much stronger terms about the situation that was occurring?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Colonel Mrksic in greater detail than described here, so if necessary, I can give you the details. I told him where I was, what I did, what I saw, and what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You didn't say to him, sir: You know, it would be a nice thing if we just send someone to offer some advice to Colonel Vojnovic. You said to him that there's a serious threat to the prisoners right now. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The essence is identical. The situation is serious. It would be good if somebody went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if we go to paragraph 86 of your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. It's on page 23, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said, and I'll read the paragraph: "After spending about 15 minutes at Ovcara, I went to the OG South command post in Negoslavci where I arrived at around 1530 hours. I reported to Colonel Mrksic and informed him about the decision of the SAO SBZS government to prosecute prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital and about my preparations for the visit of reporters and about what I had seen at Ovcara. In connection with Ovcara, I told him that the prisoners were at Ovcara but that there were no representatives of the SAO SBZS authorities, even though they said they'd be holding trials at Ovcara. I also told Mrksic I had doubts about the safety of the prisoners at Ovcara. I'm not sure whether I mentioned to Mrksic that the prisoners were under the protection of the 80th Motorised Brigade." Is that correct, sir, what was said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it would be good if there were questions reflected here to which I gave my answers. I don't know why this last sentence was inserted here. It is outside of the context, but the fact is that this is my statement. It is needless to say that Vojnovic was at Ovcara and that that was his area of responsibility. I don't see why this last sentence was inserted here. Perhaps it could be clear if we could see the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, could you go to the paragraph just above the last two sentences of paragraph 85. Right above that, you state in those last two sentences before paragraph 85: "I do not know why Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic and his military police were at Ovcara. I can only assume that Colonel Mrksic ordered them to be there."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 80th Brigade had Ovcara in its area of responsibility, and it was logical for them to secure the place, just as they provided security to the previous groups. So I don't understand why I gave that comment. The fact is that they were there and that they did that job. Perhaps it has to do with translation. Perhaps the meaning was misrecorded. I wasn't sure that there was some other order issued by Mrksic to Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you mention "orders from Mrksic to Vojnovic." You were aware, sir, that the 80th Motorised Brigade was subordinated to Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as a result, you knew that Colonel Vojnovic took orders from Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, also in that paragraph, where you believe that Colonel Mrksic might have ordered the 80th to be there, you state, if you look in the middle, that you mention those people and you say: "They were walking up and down the path leading to the hangar at Ovcara. I do not think they represented a threat to the 80th Motorised Brigade, but they may have been a threat to the prisoners at Ovcara. Vojnovic and I concluded that the security of the prisoners might not be sufficient. While I was at Ovcara, I did not see Major Sljivancanin, but I remember seeing his deputy, Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic." Is that also correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you, at that point, believed that there was a threat to the prisoners, and did you convey this belief to Colonel Mrksic that there was a threat or serious threat to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed that they needed to check the security detail and reinforce it and I said that I thought that somebody ought to be sent there whose specialty it was, so that they could make appropriate corrections, and I concluded the same with Vojnovic, namely, that security needed to be reinforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you state in paragraph 86 as part of that that you told Mrksic that you had doubts about the safety of those prisoners at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you wanted someone to evaluate the situation, if you look at page 87, "... to make sure that the safety of the prisoners was guaranteed." Those are your words. Paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 93, you continue discussing this. It's on page 24 in the English, I'm not sure on the B/C/S. 24 on the B/C/S. Thank you. "On 20th of November, 1991, Colonel Mrksic had all the information necessary to make appropriate decisions to ensure the safety of prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital. There were no interruptions in the system of command and control or the reporting system that could have prevented him from receiving the most recent information that day. Considering my feelings about the local Serbian TO and the fact that Colonel Mrksic knew about the threat to the safety of the prisoners posed by the local TO, he could have used units of the Guards Motorised Brigade to neutralise or eliminate this threat. The local Serbian TO was no match for the Guards Motorised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So according to your statement, you advised Colonel Mrksic of the threat to the safety of those prisoners and nothing was done to neutralise or eliminate this threat; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, and I think that he reacted. I think he did send some people to Ovcara, but I cannot be certain about it and I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you can say for certain that he never sent members of either of the two military police battalions or members of the Guards Motorised Brigade infantry battalions to protect those prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't send a unit. He knows this best. There was probably no need for that. Vojnovic had a military police company. He had an artillery battalion there. And to put it briefly, he had sufficient forces to secure the place himself. What was needed there was a specialist presence to give suggestions and advice; otherwise, the forces that Vojnovic had were sufficient to protect them. I think that it was not rational to deploy another unit when there was no other task in that area of responsibility except to secure a facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Major Vukasinovic was there, the deputy security organ, and he was there while prisoners were being mistreated. That shows there was a serious problem. Colonel Mrksic did not send members of the Guards Motorised Brigade. In your words: "He could have used units of the Guards Motorised Brigade to neutralise or eliminate this threat." But he did not do that; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct he could have sent, but at that moment, Vojnovic alone was capable of completing this task without additional units. I saw Major Vukasinovic but I don't know what task was assigned to him. I left and he remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present when Major Vukasinovic notified Colonel Mrksic of the mistreatment of prisoners at Ovcara and Mrksic did nothing? Were you present for that at the command post at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that incident, and I never described it and I would have if I remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Moore is in the hallway outside the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good, I was about to say, he's overstayed his time and we've run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Alas he appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour mentioned certain administrative matters. Yesterday, I wanted them to be clarified today. I am in a position to do so. I don't know if the witness needs to remain. It's entirely for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our problem is time. You were wanting five minutes or so and we've now got less than two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For two days, we've overrun our time and delayed the following trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do it, I hope, in two minutes because I've spoken to the Defence about various matters. I understood there was agreement but we'll see. Your Honour, the situation is as follows: The evidence on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin should conclude in the week ending the 8th of December although I believe the date is the 6th of December, but I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was in error, it is the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. So Mr. Lukic can just have his heart rate drop a little. So that is the 8th of December. If there are going to be recall of any witnesses or peripheral matters, that clearly has to be done with the week ending the 15th of December because we go into the recess period and that may well be an aspect that will arise. The court recess is from the 18th of December until the week ending, I think, the 5th of January, but of course there is the Serbian new year, and therefore I think my learned friends had indicated that it would be difficult for them to come before the court, of course, entirely at the Court's behest, but that would be about the 7th or 8th. We are considering possible rebuttal evidence and I don't know if it would find favour with the Court if we tried to set aside a period and that would be the 12th to the 17th of January inclusive. I know that my learned friends, perhaps with the exception of Mr. Borovic, agree with that particular proposal. The closing brief, I know again, that all parties conclude that they would wish to have one month. So if it was mid-January, that would be until mid-February, and can I just suggest, perhaps, the 19th of February and then again my learned friends are in agreement that preparation for closing argument would take no more than two weeks. So therefore, closing arguments, if the Court were agreeable, that could be the 28th of February, which is a Wednesday, the 1st of March, and I think the 2nd of March because my learned friends again consider, and I agree with them, that it would be prudent to have three days for closing arguments. That would therefore mean that the whole case would conclude by the 2nd of March. We have tried to put into this timetable all eventualities and in our submission, I believe it is a joint submission, that this timetable would be beneficial to the preparation of the case as a whole, and I don't know if that would find favour with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Is there anything that anybody wants to suggest contrary to that? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not contrary, just a clarification of our arguments, at least mine, but I think that my colleagues agree. We are trying to abide by the plan and we hope to conclude by the date given by you. Our first proposal is, if we have an extra two or three days at around that time, and if it is possible to call back the witness that we mentioned, then it might be prudent to take advantage of those extra two or three days. As for rebuttal and rejoinder, we can talk about that only later. What's important for our Defence team and also for my colleagues is that as soon as the case is over, we need about four working weeks to prepare the final brief. I think it's important for all the parties, and regardless of the conclusion of the trial, I think that we need a period of four weeks for the preparation of the final brief. I think it's important both for the Defence and for the OTP. We also agreed that three days would be sufficient for closing arguments, and we would need three weeks in between in order to prepare. So we are in full agreement with the Prosecution regarding that. We would just like to ask you to bear in mind this request of ours that we need a good four weeks to prepare our final briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since I consulted Mr. Lukic, who told me that he might even conclude by the 6th of December his case, if the Court should decide that the additional witness can be examined, that that be done on the 7th and 8th. As for the rest, I hesitate to raise any concerns because I do not like to be the only one objecting constantly. I'll leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing to add in order not to use up any more time. I fully agree with what everybody's said and we had agreed on that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would thank counsel. We will consider what you have put to us. Can we indicate the more pressing matter? That is, assuming that Mr. Lukic finishes by the 8th of December, we would certainly hope to hear any recalled witness, and there are still issues to be resolved there, either at the end of that week if there's time, or into the next week, early in the next week. The question of rebuttal witnesses is a more complex and more lengthy one, but if we can finish the primary case before we break for the festive season, that would be a good idea. We certainly take note of the Serbian celebrations and would not sit until they are passed, so that people can plan their break there. Thank you very much, and once again, I've got to go and apologise to the next Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
